pronunciation.approximation: 'LAY-toh' — hold the first vowel long like 'lay' without the off-glide, and let the final 'oh' carry a gentle rise-and-fall pitch.

pronunciation.note: Lētō is Tier 1: the Greek original contains both length (ē and ō) and the circumflex pitch contour. The English 'Leto' preserves neither.

domains.title: Mother of the Divine Twins
domains.subtitle: Night, Refuge, and the Letoön
domains.lead: Lētō is the mother of Apollo and Artemis, pursued across land and sea by Hera's jealousy, and at last given refuge by the floating island of Delos. She is the goddess of the hidden journey, the patience of motherhood, and the sanctuary that becomes holy because it sheltered the gods.

cards.name: Mother of Twins
cards.desc: She bore Apollo and Artemis, the archer gods of light and wilderness.

cards.name: Refugee Goddess
cards.desc: Hera denied her a fixed birthplace; Delos alone offered sanctuary.

cards.name: Letoön
cards.desc: Her great sanctuary near Xanthos in Lycia, shared with her children.

cards.name: Chthonic Mother
cards.desc: Her links to night and Lycian cults give her a darker, older dimension.

mythology.lead: Lētō's mythology is dominated by one of the most famous birth narratives in Greek religion: the persecution of a pregnant goddess and the founding of a holy island.

myths.title: The Wanderings of Lētō
myths.text: Hera, furious that Zeus had fathered children by Lētō, sent the serpent Pýthōn to pursue her and forbade any land under the sun to receive her. Lētō wandered through many lands until she reached Delos, a barren, floating island. The island trembled at first, fearing Apollo's wrath, but Lētō swore that her son would make it famous and rich. There, clinging to a palm tree, she gave birth first to Artemis and then, with Artemis's help, to Apollo.

myths.title: Latona and the Lycian Peasants
myths.text: In Ovid's version, the thirsty Latona stopped at a Lycian pool to drink. Local peasants stirred the mud to prevent her. In anger she transformed them into frogs, condemning them to croak forever in the mire. The story explains the croaking of frogs and warns against insulting a goddess in need.

myths.title: The Letoon of Lycia
myths.text: At the Letoon near Xanthos, Lētō was worshipped alongside Apollo and Artemis as a triad. The site was so important that its priests could grant asylum, and the Lycian confederation held meetings there. The great Xanthos trilingual inscription was set up to honour the sanctuary, linking Greek, Lycian, and Aramaic conceptions of the goddess.

lore.syncretism: The Romans knew Lētō as Latona, and her cult spread through Italy with that of Apollo. In Lycia she was identified with a local mother goddess, Lada, and the Letoon became a centre of syncretic worship. Later European art remembered her chiefly through the story of Latona and the Lycian peasants, a favourite subject of Baroque painters exploring divine wrath and metamorphosis.
lore.culturalLegacy: Lētō's most enduring legacy is Delos itself, one of the most important archaeological sites in Greece and a UNESCO World Heritage centre. Her story of persecution and sanctuary also resonates in later narratives of divine mothers and exiled queens. The name Leto appears in literature, astronomy, and even botany (the lotus is sometimes called the lotos in her honour), while her Roman form Latona adorns fountains and gardens across Europe.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Lētō is the goddess of the difficult birth. Hounded, homeless, and in labour, she finds the one place willing to receive her and makes it the axis of the Greek world. Her story is a reminder that holiness often begins in refusal: every other island said no, and so Delos became yes.

She is also the mother who disappears behind her children. Apollo and Artemis take the myths; Lētō takes the labour. To remember her is to remember the hidden work that makes glory possible—the wandering, the waiting, the palm tree, the sweat. The divine twins were born because she would not stop looking for a place to rest.
lore.originalScriptNote: The Greek is Λητώ. The first vowel is eta (ē), long [eː]; the final omega (ō) is long [ɔː] with a circumflex accent indicating a falling pitch on a long vowel. The Roman form Latona loses both the vowel length and the pitch contour. PUNYCODEX restores Lētō with the macron on ē and the circumflex on ō, since the full Greek breathing marks are not registrable.
